screens.title: Learning Objectives — Foundations
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives define concrete skills you will practice and why each matters in real operations. First, you will explain the importance of user accounts and authentication for device security. That means understanding how weak access controls can permit unauthorized configuration changes or outages, and how auditing depends on unique user identities. Second, you will create and configure local user accounts on Junos OS devices. You will practice the exact configuration commands and learn the steps to set a strong password and commit changes. Third, you will understand the different user classes and their permissions. This helps you assign the least privilege needed for tasks and prevents accidental destructive actions. Fourth, you will differentiate between local and remote authentication methods such as RADIUS and TACACS+, and know when to centralize accounts for scale. Each objective links to practical operational improvements: stronger access control, easier audits, and fewer shared credentials. As you work, notice common pitfalls like shared accounts and excessive super-user privileges, and plan to remove or disable inactive accounts as part of routine maintenance.

screens.title: Why user accounts and authentication matter
screens.narratorSegment: Device security depends on strong access controls. When accounts are missing or weak, anyone with console or network access can make configuration changes, potentially causing outages or exposing data. User accounts provide unique identities so actions are attributable and auditable. Authentication verifies those identities, and authorization — the user class — decides what each identity can do. A simple example: if two technicians share a single account, you cannot tell which person changed an interface setting during incident response. Centralized authentication systems improve this because they keep a single authoritative record of users and their attributes. A common misconception is that local accounts alone are sufficient for all environments. While local accounts are appropriate in small deployments or as a fallback, they become hard to manage at scale and may lead to inconsistent password rules or forgotten inactive accounts. The practical takeaway is to use unique local accounts for administrators, enforce strong passwords, and plan migration to centralized authentication for larger fleets. Reflect: when was the last time inactive accounts were audited in your environment, and who would you contact to remove them?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Security Rationale
Why user accounts and authentication matter
Accounts provide identity; authentication confirms it; classes limit what identities can do.
  • Unique accounts make actions attributable for troubleshooting and audits.
  • Authentication prevents unauthorized access and reduces the chance of accidental misconfiguration.
  • Authorization via user classes enforces least privilege and reduces blast radius of mistakes.
  • Centralized servers reduce administrative overhead and ensure consistent policies across many devices.
Example
Two people sharing one account prevents auditing. Unique accounts link changes to an individual for accountability.
Common mistake
Leaving default or weak passwords or failing to disable inactive accounts.
Key Takeaway

Treat accounts as identities: assign unique users, validate them, and restrict their permissions to what they need.

Operational impact
Better access controls reduce mean time to repair and make security investigations straightforward.
Reflection
When scaling beyond a handful of devices, plan for centralized authentication to avoid inconsistent policies.

screens.title: Create a local user on Junos OS
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a local user on Junos OS is a simple, repeatable process that you will practice until it becomes second nature. Begin by entering configuration mode. Then navigate under the system login hierarchy and use the set system login user command with the user's class and authentication method. The device will prompt you to enter and confirm a password when using plain-text-password. After setting the user, always run commit to apply the change. A concrete example from the chapter shows creating junior-admin with read-only privileges and a strong password. After commit, exit configuration mode and test by logging in as that user. Confirm that read-only commands work and that configuration mode is denied. A misconception to avoid is expecting immediate privilege escalation; class membership determines allowed commands and must be chosen carefully. In practice, use unique accounts per administrator, document the purpose of each account, and immediately disable any temporary or test accounts when no longer needed. This practice keeps your device audit trail useful and your operations safer. Create a local user on Junos OS means use set system login user <name> class <class> authentication plain-text-password, then commit and test the account.. In practical terms, step-by-step cli commands and commit workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Local User Creation
Create a local user on Junos OS
Follow these commands in configuration mode and test the new account.
# Log in as root or a super-user and enter configuration mode
user@router> configure

# Create a new user with read-only class
set system login user junior-admin class read-only authentication plain-text-password
# You will be prompted to enter and confirm the password: ReadOnly#1

# Commit the change
commit

# Exit configuration mode
exit
exit

# Test the account by logging in as 'junior-admin' and run show configuration (allowed)
# Attempt to enter configuration mode with 'configure' (should fail)
Example
The sample code above creates junior-admin with read-only privileges and shows the commit and test steps.
Common mistake
Forgetting to commit after configuration changes means the user will not exist at runtime.
Test scenario
Log in as the new user and verify allowed commands like show configuration and that configure is denied.
Key Takeaway
Always test a newly created account immediately to confirm class-based permissions.

screens.title: User classes and permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Junos OS uses user classes to group permissions and make assignment easier. The standard classes are super-user, operator, read-only, and unauthorized. Super-user grants full read-write access to configuration and operational commands; treat it like a root account and assign it sparingly. Operator is intended for operational troubleshooting and monitoring; it permits many operational commands but does not allow configuration changes. Read-only permits viewing of configuration and operational data but prevents any modification. Unauthorized authenticates a user but grants no CLI access. You can also create custom classes that allow a defined set of commands, which is essential to implement least-privilege policies. For example, a junior support account could be granted only interface statistics and ping commands. A common misconception is that operator and read-only are interchangeable; they are not — operator often includes operational tools that a pure read-only account lacks. Use custom classes when the built-in roles are too coarse, and document their allowed commands so audits can verify compliance. The core benefit of classes is predictable, auditable permission mapping for users. User classes and permissions means user classes map identities to allowed commands. use built-ins for common roles and custom classes for least-privilege needs.. In practical terms, what each standard class allows and why you would use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › User Classes
User classes and permissions
Standard classes define what a user may see and do on the device.
super-user
Full read-write access to configuration and operational commands. Use only for trusted admins.
operator
Access to operational commands for monitoring and diagnostics, but cannot change configuration.
read-only
View-only access to configuration and operational state; cannot alter settings.
unauthorized
User is authenticated but granted no CLI access; useful for limited authentication checks.
Custom classes
Define a list of allowed CLI commands or hierarchy levels to tailor permissions for specific job functions.
Analogy
Think of classes as keycards: each card opens a defined set of doors. Custom cards let you open only the doors needed for a role.
Key Takeaway
Match user classes to job duties and prefer least privilege to limit accidental or malicious changes.

screens.title: Local accounts vs. remote authentication
screens.narratorSegment: Local user accounts store usernames and passwords directly on the Junos device. They are easy to configure and useful for small deployments or as a fallback when network connectivity to a server is unavailable. However, they become burdensome to maintain across many devices because each device needs the same user entries and consistent password policies must be manually applied. Remote authentication methods—RADIUS and TACACS+—centralize user management. RADIUS is an open-standard protocol that combines authentication and authorization and is widely used for network access control. TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct functions, offering more flexibility for granular command authorization. The practical advantage of centralization is a single point of truth for user accounts, easier enforcement of password policies, and improved auditing. A common mistake is assuming remote authentication removes the need for local users; instead, keep local accounts as a configured fallback and explicitly set the authentication order to define fallback behavior. Consider scale and auditing requirements when choosing the right approach. Local accounts vs. remote authentication means use local users for small deployments or fallback; centralize with radius/tacacs+ where many devices require consistent policies and audit logs.. In practical terms, when to store users locally and when to centralize. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Local vs Remote Auth
Local accounts vs. remote authentication
Compare trade-offs to pick the right approach for your network.
Local users
Stored on the device, simple to configure, ideal for small sites or emergency fallback.
Remote servers
Centralized management with consistent policies, easier audits, better scalability.
Best practice
Configure authentication-order so the device knows whether to try remote servers first and when to fall back to local accounts.
Example scenario
Large deployments with hundreds of devices benefit from RADIUS or TACACS+ to enforce a single password policy.
Pitfall
Relying solely on remote servers without a local fallback can lock you out if network issues occur; keep local accounts as a safe fallback.

screens.title: RADIUS and TACACS+ overview
screens.narratorSegment: RADIUS and TACACS+ are the two primary remote authentication approaches used with network devices. RADIUS is an open standard that typically combines authentication and authorization in a single step and is widely used for network access control such as Wi-Fi and VPNs. It provides a straightforward way to authenticate users and pass back attributes about their session. TACACS+, on the other hand, separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct functions. This separation allows TACACS+ to offer more granular command authorization per user, which is especially useful for device administration where you want to control which CLI commands a user can run. The chapter notes that TACACS+ is popular for device administration due to its flexible AAA model. A practical misconception to avoid is assuming RADIUS and TACACS+ are interchangeable: choose RADIUS for broader network access control needs, and TACACS+ when fine-grained device command authorization and detailed accounting are required. Both approaches centralize user databases, simplify policy enforcement, and improve auditing compared to local accounts alone. RADIUS and TACACS+ overview means use radius for standard network access workflows and tacacs+ for granular device administration and command authorization when needed.. In practical terms, core differences and when each protocol is commonly used. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

RADIUS and TACACS+ overview
Understand protocol differences and operational uses.
RADIUS
An open-standard protocol that combines authentication and authorization, commonly used for network access such as Wi-Fi and VPNs.
TACACS+
Separates authentication, authorization, and accounting for granular command control and flexible device administration.
Practical note
Choose the protocol that matches your need for centralization versus per-command authorization control.
Example
Use RADIUS to authenticate remote VPN users and TACACS+ to authorize which CLI commands administrators may perform.
Key Takeaway
Both centralize authentication; TACACS+ is better for granular device command control, RADIUS for broad network access.

screens.title: Authentication order and fallback
screens.narratorSegment: Authentication order determines the sequence a Junos device uses to validate credentials. You can configure the device to try remote methods first and then fall back to local accounts, or vice versa. For example, setting authentication-order to radius password instructs the device to try RADIUS before local passwords. Choosing an appropriate order matters operationally: if you prefer centralized control but need local fallback during server outages, configure remote first with local second. Conversely, if local emergency accounts must always be available, put password first. A typical misconception is that setting remote authentication removes local accounts entirely; it does not — it only changes the attempt sequence. Always test your authentication order by simulating remote server unavailability and confirming that local fallback works as expected. Record the chosen order in runbooks so operators know how logins will behave during outages. This simple configuration reduces lockout risk and ensures predictable behavior during maintenance windows. Authentication order and fallback means configure the order such as radius password so the device tries preferred servers first and local accounts as fallbacks.. In practical terms, how junos decides where to authenticate and what to try next. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Authentication Order
Authentication order and fallback
Define which methods the device tries and in what sequence.
Command example
set system authentication-order [ radius password ]
This example tries RADIUS first, then falls back to the local password database.
Best practice
Define a fallback strategy and test it during simulated server downtime.
Pitfall
Assuming remote servers are always available; without fallback you risk administrative lockout.
Runbook tip
Document authentication order and test steps to recover when servers are unreachable.
Key Takeaway
Choose authentication order to balance centralized control with safe local fallback during outages.

screens.title: Password policy options in Junos OS
screens.narratorSegment: Junos OS provides password-options to enforce basic password policies on local accounts. Typical settings include minimum length and complexity rules — for example, requiring a minimum of ten characters or mixed-case with numbers and symbols. screens.title: Centralized authentication architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Centralized authentication places a server or cluster of servers in your network that act as the authoritative source for user accounts. Junos devices are configured with the server IP addresses and an authentication order. When a user logs in, the device forwards credentials to the server and receives a pass or fail response along with any authorized attributes. With TACACS+, the device can receive separate authorization decisions for commands, enabling per-command control. In practice, deploy redundant servers and configure devices with multiple server addresses so authentication survives a single server failure. Document shared secrets and ensure secure connectivity between devices and servers. A misconception is that centralization removes all device-level responsibility; you still need emergency local accounts and a tested fallback plan. Centralized authentication improves auditing because all logs and accounting records can be centralized; that makes compliance or incident investigation far easier than hunting through dozens of device local logs. Consider scale, redundancy, and runbooks when designing your authentication architecture. screens.title: Common mistakes and operational hygiene
screens.narratorSegment: Operational hygiene for accounts prevents many security incidents. Common mistakes include using default or weak passwords, sharing accounts among multiple people, granting super-user privileges too broadly, and leaving inactive accounts enabled. Each of these practices undermines auditing and increases the chance of accidental or malicious configuration changes. The recommended countermeasures are straightforward: assign unique accounts, apply least privilege with appropriate classes, enforce sensible password policies, and regularly review and disable accounts that are no longer needed. For larger environments, centralize user management and auditing with RADIUS or TACACS+ to avoid inconsistent rules. Another frequent oversight is failing to document temporary elevation of privileges; always record when you grant higher privileges and remove them as soon as the task is complete. Run a periodic audit that lists active accounts, their classes, and last login dates so stale accounts can be disabled. These small routines dramatically reduce risk and make incident response far simpler. fullNarratorScript:
Securing device access begins with clear user accounts and strong authentication. In this lesson you will see why user accounts are the first line of defense on Junos devices, how to create a local account, what user classes control, and when to centralize authentication with RADIUS or TACACS+. We will walk through the exact Junos configuration commands used to add a local user and set a password, explain the practical differences between super-user, operator, and read-only roles, and show how centralized servers simplify administration at scale. You will also learn basic password options you can enforce to reduce risk, and common mistakes to avoid such as sharing accounts or leaving inactive accounts enabled. By the end, you should be able to create a secure local user, pick an appropriate class for their duties, and decide whether remote authentication is right for your environment. Think about an environment with many devices: how would a central server change your workflow? That question helps frame the value of the techniques you will practice here.

These objectives define concrete skills you will practice and why each matters in real operations. First, you will explain the importance of user accounts and authentication for device security. That means understanding how weak access controls can permit unauthorized configuration changes or outages, and how auditing depends on unique user identities. Second, you will create and configure local user accounts on Junos OS devices. You will practice the exact configuration commands and learn the steps to set a strong password and commit changes. Third, you will understand the different user classes and their permissions. This helps you assign the least privilege needed for tasks and prevents accidental destructive actions. Fourth, you will differentiate between local and remote authentication methods such as RADIUS and TACACS+, and know when to centralize accounts for scale. Each objective links to practical operational improvements: stronger access control, easier audits, and fewer shared credentials. As you work, notice common pitfalls like shared accounts and excessive super-user privileges, and plan to remove or disable inactive accounts as part of routine maintenance.

Now that you know the skill targets, we'll describe what mastery looks like operationally. You will be able to create a local user and verify its access, meaning you can add the user, set a strong password, commit the configuration, and then test login and permitted commands. You will understand user classes well enough to assign the correct class for a technician who only needs monitoring commands. You will be able to explain the trade-offs between local credentials and remote authentication like RADIUS and TACACS+, including how centralized servers simplify password policy enforcement and auditing. Finally, you will apply basic password-options on a Junos device, setting minimum-length and complexity rules so that all local users meet defined requirements. Each milestone includes a verification action: log in as the new user, try an operation beyond their class, and confirm the expected denial. These checks reduce surprises in production and make audits straightforward.

Device security depends on strong access controls. When accounts are missing or weak, anyone with console or network access can make configuration changes, potentially causing outages or exposing data. User accounts provide unique identities so actions are attributable and auditable. Authentication verifies those identities, and authorization — the user class — decides what each identity can do. A simple example: if two technicians share a single account, you cannot tell which person changed an interface setting during incident response. Centralized authentication systems improve this because they keep a single authoritative record of users and their attributes. A common misconception is that local accounts alone are sufficient for all environments. While local accounts are appropriate in small deployments or as a fallback, they become hard to manage at scale and may lead to inconsistent password rules or forgotten inactive accounts. The practical takeaway is to use unique local accounts for administrators, enforce strong passwords, and plan migration to centralized authentication for larger fleets. Reflect: when was the last time inactive accounts were audited in your environment, and who would you contact to remove them?

Creating a local user on Junos OS is a simple, repeatable process that you will practice until it becomes second nature. Begin by entering configuration mode. Then navigate under the system login hierarchy and use the set system login user command with the user's class and authentication method. The device will prompt you to enter and confirm a password when using plain-text-password. After setting the user, always run commit to apply the change. A concrete example from the chapter shows creating junior-admin with read-only privileges and a strong password. After commit, exit configuration mode and test by logging in as that user. Confirm that read-only commands work and that configuration mode is denied. A misconception to avoid is expecting immediate privilege escalation; class membership determines allowed commands and must be chosen carefully. In practice, use unique accounts per administrator, document the purpose of each account, and immediately disable any temporary or test accounts when no longer needed. This practice keeps your device audit trail useful and your operations safer. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Junos OS uses user classes to group permissions and make assignment easier. The standard classes are super-user, operator, read-only, and unauthorized. Super-user grants full read-write access to configuration and operational commands; treat it like a root account and assign it sparingly. Operator is intended for operational troubleshooting and monitoring; it permits many operational commands but does not allow configuration changes. Read-only permits viewing of configuration and operational data but prevents any modification. Unauthorized authenticates a user but grants no CLI access. You can also create custom classes that allow a defined set of commands, which is essential to implement least-privilege policies. For example, a junior support account could be granted only interface statistics and ping commands. A common misconception is that operator and read-only are interchangeable; they are not — operator often includes operational tools that a pure read-only account lacks. Use custom classes when the built-in roles are too coarse, and document their allowed commands so audits can verify compliance. The core benefit of classes is predictable, auditable permission mapping for users. Local user accounts store usernames and passwords directly on the Junos device. They are easy to configure and useful for small deployments or as a fallback when network connectivity to a server is unavailable. However, they become burdensome to maintain across many devices because each device needs the same user entries and consistent password policies must be manually applied. Remote authentication methods—RADIUS and TACACS+—centralize user management. RADIUS is an open-standard protocol that combines authentication and authorization and is widely used for network access control. TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct functions, offering more flexibility for granular command authorization. The practical advantage of centralization is a single point of truth for user accounts, easier enforcement of password policies, and improved auditing. A common mistake is assuming remote authentication removes the need for local users; instead, keep local accounts as a configured fallback and explicitly set the authentication order to define fallback behavior. Consider scale and auditing requirements when choosing the right approach. RADIUS and TACACS+ are the two primary remote authentication approaches used with network devices. RADIUS is an open standard that typically combines authentication and authorization in a single step and is widely used for network access control such as Wi-Fi and VPNs. It provides a straightforward way to authenticate users and pass back attributes about their session. TACACS+, on the other hand, separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct functions. This separation allows TACACS+ to offer more granular command authorization per user, which is especially useful for device administration where you want to control which CLI commands a user can run. The chapter notes that TACACS+ is popular for device administration due to its flexible AAA model. A practical misconception to avoid is assuming RADIUS and TACACS+ are interchangeable: choose RADIUS for broader network access control needs, and TACACS+ when fine-grained device command authorization and detailed accounting are required. Both approaches centralize user databases, simplify policy enforcement, and improve auditing compared to local accounts alone. Authentication order determines the sequence a Junos device uses to validate credentials. You can configure the device to try remote methods first and then fall back to local accounts, or vice versa. For example, setting authentication-order to radius password instructs the device to try RADIUS before local passwords. Choosing an appropriate order matters operationally: if you prefer centralized control but need local fallback during server outages, configure remote first with local second. Conversely, if local emergency accounts must always be available, put password first. A typical misconception is that setting remote authentication removes local accounts entirely; it does not — it only changes the attempt sequence. Centralized authentication places a server or cluster of servers in your network that act as the authoritative source for user accounts. Junos devices are configured with the server IP addresses and an authentication order. When a user logs in, the device forwards credentials to the server and receives a pass or fail response along with any authorized attributes. With TACACS+, the device can receive separate authorization decisions for commands, enabling per-command control. In practice, deploy redundant servers and configure devices with multiple server addresses so authentication survives a single server failure. Operational hygiene for accounts prevents many security incidents. Common mistakes include using default or weak passwords, sharing accounts among multiple people, granting super-user privileges too broadly, and leaving inactive accounts enabled. Each of these practices undermines auditing and increases the chance of accidental or malicious configuration changes. The recommended countermeasures are straightforward: assign unique accounts, apply least privilege with appropriate classes, enforce sensible password policies, and regularly review and disable accounts that are no longer needed. For larger environments, centralize user management and auditing with RADIUS or TACACS+ to avoid inconsistent rules. Another frequent oversight is failing to document temporary elevation of privileges; always record when you grant higher privileges and remove them as soon as the task is complete. Run a periodic audit that lists active accounts, their classes, and last login dates so stale accounts can be disabled. These small routines dramatically reduce risk and make incident response far simpler. Let's summarize three essential concepts to remember. First, a local user account stores username, password, and class directly on the Junos device and is useful for small deployments or emergency fallback. Second, a user class is a predefined or custom set of permissions that controls which CLI commands and configuration hierarchies a user may access; apply least privilege when assigning classes. Third, super-user is the class granting full administrative privileges; assign it sparingly because it allows complete configuration changes. Keep these definitions in mind as you create accounts, design roles, and document auditing procedures.
